q: Oxidation numbers have a variety of uses in chemistry- from writing formulae to predicting properties of compounds and assisting in the balancing of ____ reactions in which electrons are transferred.
e: Oxidation numbers are essential for balancing redox reactions where electron transfer occurs.

q: The ____ (or oxidation state) of an atom can be zero, positive, or negative.
e: The oxidation number represents the number of electrons lost or gained by an atom.

q: All elements in their free state (uncombined with other elements) have an oxidation number of ____.
e: Free neutral atoms have the same number of electrons assigned to them as in their free state, resulting in an oxidation number of zero.

q: A positive oxidation number means the atom has ____ electrons assigned to it than in the neutral atom.
e: A positive oxidation number indicates the number of electrons removed from a neutral atom.

q: A negative oxidation number means the atom has ____ electrons assigned to it than in the neutral atom.
e: A negative oxidation number indicates the number of electrons added to a neutral atom.

q: The oxidation number of an atom that has lost or gained electrons to form an ion is the same as the positive or negative ____ of the ion.
e: The oxidation state of a monatomic ion is equal to its net electrical charge.

q: All elements regardless of whether they are monoatomic, diatomic or triatomic have an oxidation number of ____.
e: Elements in their free, uncombined state always have an oxidation number of zero.

q: The algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of the atoms in a neutral molecule is ____.
e: For any electrically neutral compound, the sum of all oxidation numbers must equal zero.

q: The algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of the atoms in a polyatomic ion is equal to the ____ on the ion.
e: The sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion must equal the net charge of that ion.

q: Oxidation number of H is ____, except in metal hydrides, where it is -1.
e: Hydrogen generally has an oxidation number of +1 when combined with nonmetals.

q: Oxidation number of H in metal hydrides is ____.
e: In metal hydrides like NaH or CaH2, hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal and takes an oxidation state of -1.

q: Oxidation number of O is ____, except in peroxides and in $OF_2$.
e: Oxygen typically has an oxidation number of -2 in most of its compounds.

q: Oxidation number of O in peroxides (e.g., $H_2O_2$, $BaO_2$, $Na_2O_2$) is ____.
e: In peroxide compounds, the oxygen atoms share a different bonding arrangement, resulting in an oxidation state of -1.

q: Oxidation number of O in $OF_2$ is ____.
e: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so oxygen takes a positive oxidation state of +2 in $OF_2$.

q: The metallic element in an ionic compound has a ____ oxidation number.
e: Metals tend to lose electrons to form cations, resulting in a positive oxidation number.

q: Alkali metals in combined state have an oxidation number ____.
e: Group 1 alkali metals always exhibit an oxidation state of +1 in their compounds.

q: Alkaline earth metals in combined state have an oxidation number ____.
e: Group 2 alkaline earth metals always exhibit an oxidation state of +2 in their compounds.

q: The oxidation number of halogen in compounds (e.g., $BaCl_2$, $NaBr$, $KI$) is ____.
e: Halogens typically have an oxidation number of -1 when combined with less electronegative elements.

q: In covalent compounds, the negative oxidation number is assigned to the more ____ atom.
e: Electrons in a covalent bond are assigned to the more electronegative atom for the purpose of determining oxidation numbers.

q: Oxidation and reduction reactions involve the transfer of oxygen atoms, or hydrogen atoms, electrons, or change in ____.
e: Redox reactions can be defined through the transfer of oxygen, hydrogen, electrons, or changes in oxidation states.

q: When a substance gains oxygen in a chemical reaction, it is ____.
e: The addition of oxygen to a substance is the classical definition of oxidation.

q: When a substance loses oxygen in a chemical reaction, it is ____.
e: The removal of oxygen from a substance is the classical definition of reduction.

q: When a substance loses hydrogen in a chemical reaction, it is ____.
e: The removal of hydrogen (an electropositive element) from a substance is considered oxidation.

q: When a substance gains hydrogen in a chemical reaction, it is ____.
e: The addition of hydrogen (an electropositive element) to a substance is considered reduction.

q: Oxidation is the addition of oxygen (or ____ element) to a substance.
e: The concept of oxidation is extended to include the addition of any electronegative element.

q: Reduction is the ____ of oxygen (or electronegative element) from a substance.
e: Reduction involves the removal of oxygen or any electronegative element from a substance.

q: Oxidation is the removal of hydrogen (or ____ element) from a substance.
e: Oxidation can also be defined as the removal of hydrogen or any electropositive element.

q: Oxidation is the ____ of electrons by an element, compound or ion.
e: In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is defined as the loss of electrons.

q: Reduction is the ____ of electrons by an element, compound or ion.
e: In terms of electron transfer, reduction is defined as the gain of electrons.

q: Any element which increases in oxidation number is said to be ____.
e: An increase in oxidation number indicates a loss of electrons, which is oxidation.

q: Any element which decreases in oxidation number is said to be ____.
e: A decrease in oxidation number indicates a gain of electrons, which is reduction.

q: Chemical reactions which involve oxidation as well as reduction processes simultaneously, are known as ____.
e: Redox reactions are characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of oxidation and reduction.

q: The separate oxidation and reduction reactions are called ____.
e: Chemists describe the oxidation and reduction components of a redox reaction separately as half-reactions.

q: Redox reactions require a track of each ____ to each atom in chemical reactions.
e: Balancing redox reactions requires keeping track of electron transfer to each atom involved.

q: An oxidising agent or oxidant is an ____ of electrons and is reduced itself in a chemical reaction.
e: An oxidising agent accepts electrons from another substance, thereby getting reduced.

q: The oxidising agent is normally in one of its ____ possible oxidation states because it will gain electrons and be reduced.
e: Oxidising agents are typically in higher oxidation states, allowing them to gain electrons and be reduced.

q: Examples of oxidising agents include oxygen, halogens, concentrated sulphuric acid, nitric acid, hydrogen peroxide, ____, potassium dichromate, metallic oxides, etc.
e: Potassium permanganate ($KMnO_4$) is a strong and common oxidising agent used in redox reactions.

q: A reducing agent or reductant is a ____ of electrons and is oxidised itself in a chemical reaction.
e: A reducing agent donates electrons to another substance, thereby getting oxidised.

q: The reducing agent is typically in one of its ____ possible oxidation states because it will lose electrons and be oxidised in the redox reaction.
e: Reducing agents are typically in lower oxidation states, allowing them to lose electrons and be oxidised.

q: Examples of reducing agents include carbon, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, hydrogen, hydrogen sulphide, ____, etc.
e: Metals are good reducing agents because they readily lose electrons to form positive ions.

q: One way to balance oxidation-reduction equations is by keeping track of the electron transfer using the ____ of each of the atoms.
e: The oxidation number method balances redox equations by tracking changes in oxidation states.

q: Balance the oxidation number changes by multiplying appropriate coefficients to make the total increase in oxidation number ____ to the total decrease in oxidation number.
e: The total number of electrons lost must equal the total number of electrons gained.

q: In the half-equation method, the equation is separated into two ____, one for oxidation and one for reduction.
e: The ionic redox equation is split into separate oxidation and reduction half-reactions for easier balancing.

q: Balance the oxygen atoms by adding ____ molecules.
e: In aqueous redox reactions, oxygen atoms are balanced by adding $H_2O$ molecules.

q: Balance the hydrogen atoms by adding ____ ions.
e: Hydrogen atoms are balanced by adding hydrogen ions ($H^+$) in acidic conditions.

q: Balance the charge of each chemical equation with ____.
e: After balancing atoms, the net charge of each half-reaction is balanced by adding electrons.

q: The half-equations are added together, cancelling out the ____ to form one balanced chemical equation.
e: When the balanced half-reactions are combined, the electrons on both sides cancel out.

q: Acidic condition usually implies a solution with an excess of ____ concentration, hence making the solution acidic.
e: Acidic conditions are characterized by a high concentration of hydrogen ions ($H^+$).

q: Bases produce ____ ions in solution; hence, balancing a redox reaction in basic condition requires them.
e: Basic (alkaline) conditions require the use of hydroxide ions ($OH^-$) to balance the equation.

q: $OH^-$ and $H^+$ ions on the same side of a reaction should be added together to form ____.
e: In basic conditions, any remaining $H^+$ ions are neutralized by adding $OH^-$ to both sides, forming $H_2O$.
